newsitem.title: GERMANY: Deutsche Telekom rivals cry foul.
newsitem.headline: Deutsche Telekom rivals cry foul.

text.p: Two of phone giant Deutsche Telekom AG's main rivals filed regulatory complaints with the government on Monday, saying the former monopoly was using its market dominance to prevent fair competition.

The move marks the first time that the government regulator will be brought in to settle a dispute between Telekom and its rivals over the key issue of interconnection, or what price its rivals will pay to access customers over Telekom lines.

Because Telekom has enjoyed a monopoly for over a century, it is the only phone company with a network reaching into virtually every home and office and rivals are forced to lease its lines in order to cross the "last mile" to the customer.

Negotiations over the terms of this arrangement, dubbed interconnection in industry jargon, have been going on for months and many of the new phone companies getting ready for deregulation in 1998 have complained that Telekom was stalling.

Now two of the most potent Telekom rivals -- the O.Tel.O venture of utilities Veba AG and RWE AG -- and Mannesmann Arcor AG have thrown up their hands in frustration and called on government regulators to intervene.
"Telekom wants to misuse its power in the market to prevent our reaching telephone customers with better service and lower prices," said O.Tel.O chairman Ulf Bohla in a statement.

He said the complaint against Telekom filed with the Post and Telecommunications Ministry on Monday was "directed against Telekom's refusal to grant O.Tel.O direct access to the lines of end customers.
"O.Tel.O expects that it will also come to regulatory complaints regarding other details of the interconnection negotiations," the statement said.
Arcor is a joint venture of engineering group Mannesmann , the German railway, AirTouch Communications , the Unisource alliance, AT&T and Deutsche Bank .
It said in a statement nearly identical to that of O.Tel.O that it has been negotiating with Deutsche Telekom for months over the conditions for connecting their two networks.

"Without this access Arcor would lose considerable potential to market its own telephone services," the statement said. "But the former state agency consistently tries to extend its monopoly position to beyond January 1, 1998 by using all means to force through unacceptable prices and conditions."
The Post and Telecommunications Ministry, responsible for telecoms regulation until next year when a telecoms watchdog begins operating, was not immediately available for comment.
Deutsche Telekom would not comment on the substance of its competitors' claims, saying the negotiations were confidential.
"We hoped we could conclude these negotiations without the regulator," said Telekom spokesman Hans Ehnert. "Now we hope that it will still be possible to reach an agreement on time."
From the perspectives of Telekom's rivals, resorting to the regulator could be the only way to move things forward quickly.

Under Germany's brand-new telecommunications law, the government now has six weeks, with a possible extension of another four weeks, to decide on the complaint and could dictate the terms if no compromise is reached.
The German government has said it would use the United States and France among other countries as the basis for comparable market studies to determine interconnection rates.
Instead of waiting for sparks to fly, French regulators fixed a set of interconnection rates for new rivals based on a detailed analysis of costs at monopoly France Telecom.
The French rates were higher than newcomers wanted and above rates charged by British Telecom in the United Kingdom, but considerably lower than prices demanded by France Telecom.
Analysts expect rate levels set by the German government would be in the neighborhood of the French catalogue.
But then it might not get that far. The parties could withdraw their complaint if Telekom offers a better deal.
